splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be established by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that plan actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: UFCW Local 1500 Pension Fund v. Mayer Bros.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered supervision beyond what the judgment specifies when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises fundamental questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, allowing courts to find violations and revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to extend the term beyond what Congress prescribed.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the stricter gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are barred from re-raising any previously presented claim, in addition to satisfying § 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a stricter gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners under § 2255, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to election administration rules like ballot receipt deadlines. The resolution affects the ability of candidates nationwide to challenge voting procedures before elections take place, with implications for mail-in voting rules and ballot counting deadlines.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge election laws that allegedly dilute or affect the counting of lawful votes, recognizing competitive injury as sufficient.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections (lower court approach)

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge election administration rules pre-election because they fail to demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury sufficient for standing.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) in the context of criminal sentencing enhancements under the Sentencing Guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts should apply lenity or defer to the Sentencing Commission's interpretation when a Guidelines provision is ambiguous in a criminal case. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit has held that agency deference trumps lenity. The split has deepened following the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo overruling Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor deference to agency interpretations in criminal contexts, meaning ambiguous provisions must be resolved in favor of the defendant.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (Auer/Kisor) to the Sentencing Commission's commentary applies even in criminal sentencing contexts, and that lenity does not override such deference when the Commission has interpreted its own Guidelines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one is disqualifying. The split affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses and creates disparate outcomes depending on where a defendant is prosecuted.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' conjunctively as requiring each condition to be satisfied.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes, is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses is a valid, binding interpretation of an ambiguous guideline or an impermissible expansion beyond the guideline text. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy or attempt convictions qualify as career offenders under the Guidelines.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a valid interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson/Kisor, so inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text and is not entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition and cannot receive Kisor deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule criminalizes substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be federally controlled. Some circuits hold the guideline broadly encompasses any state drug offense regardless of federal scheduling, while others require a match to federal schedules.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state offenses qualify broadly
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under USSG § 4B1.2(b) encompasses state drug offenses even if the substance is not federally controlled, because the guideline text refers to 'state law' without requiring a federal match.

positions.label: Federal-law limitation applies — substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in the law can contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes, alone or combined with other factors, can never support relief, while others allow courts to consider them. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to USSG § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this, but some circuits have held the Commission exceeded its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly when combined with other factors, and that the Sentencing Commission's policy statement authorizing such consideration is valid.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must use habeas corpus rather than civil rights actions (Bivens or other statutory vehicles) to challenge the conditions or terms of their confinement, and whether habeas is the exclusive remedy for claims affecting the execution of a sentence.
splits.description: Circuits have a longstanding split on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement that affect the execution of their sentence (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement), or whether civil rights actions may also be used. This affects federal prisoners' ability to challenge BOP decisions about First Step Act time credits, transfers to prerelease custody, and other execution-of-sentence issues.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for execution-of-sentence claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the execution of a sentence, including First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody, must be brought under habeas corpus and cannot proceed as civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions are available alongside or instead of habeas
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights or Bivens actions to challenge conditions or terms of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment, even when habeas might also be available.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust and the need to protect the public.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Sentencing Reform Act permits district courts to impose revocation sentences that expressly punish defendants for their supervised release violations, or whether punishment is an impermissible sentencing purpose at revocation. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis allows express punishment, placing it at odds with other circuits.

positions.label: Punishment is a permissible purpose at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, treating the violation itself as warranting a punitive sentence.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be based on the breach of trust and the need to protect the public, not on punishing the defendant for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether property appreciation occurring between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and the conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a split with other circuits that have held it belongs to the debtor under § 348(f)(1)(A).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a), combined with § 348(f)(1)(A), means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor, not the estate, consistent with the statute's structure and legislative history protecting good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an appeal from the denial of a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that orders denying motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable as collateral orders because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. This creates tension with other circuits that have applied the collateral order doctrine more restrictively in the sealing context.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that would be irreparably lost if review is delayed until final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because litigants have other adequate means to protect privacy interests, and such orders do not satisfy the demanding 'effectively unreviewable' requirement.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, affecting hospitality, retail, and service industries. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the disagreement and clarify liability and damages standards. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for establishing discrimination liability in business establishments, making it easier for plaintiffs to prevail.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard requiring stronger proof of discriminatory intent or treatment in business establishments.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
